name: DNS
summary: The internet’s phone book: turns names into addresses.
howItWorks: DNS translates a name like `api.example.com` into an IP address. Your device asks a resolver, which answers from its cache or walks the hierarchy (the root, then `.com`, then your domain’s authoritative servers) and caches the answer for the record’s TTL. Cloud DNS services add health-checked failover and routing by latency or geography.
analogy: Calling a contact from your phone instead of memorizing their number. If they get a new number, you update the contact and every call still goes through.
useWhen: Giving every service a stable name
Failing over between regions or providers
Moving infrastructure without changing client configuration
avoidWhen: Instant cutovers: cached answers live until their TTL expires
Fine-grained load balancing, since clients cache and choose records unpredictably
example: `api.example.com` has a 60-second TTL and health-checked records in two regions. When us-east-1 fails its check, Route 53 starts answering with the us-west-2 address, and most clients follow within a minute or two.

providers.oss: BIND, CoreDNS, PowerDNS; Consul for service discovery over DNS; also Cloudflare DNS

story: On the early ARPANET, every host’s name and address lived in one file, `HOSTS.TXT`, maintained by the Network Information Center at SRI and copied by every machine over FTP. That worked while the network was a modest number of large timeshared computers. By the early 1980s it was breaking: the bandwidth spent distributing new copies grew with the square of the number of hosts, and organizations running their own local networks had to wait for the NIC to publish every change.

In November 1983 Paul Mockapetris at USC’s Information Sciences Institute proposed the Domain Name System in RFC 882 and 883. Names became a tree, split into zones that each organization runs on its own name servers, with resolvers caching answers along the way. In 1984 four Berkeley graduate students described BIND, a name server for Unix systems, and in 1987 RFC 1034 and 1035 set out the version still in use.

Later work bolted on what the original lacked. DNSSEC added signatures, and the root zone was signed in July 2010. DNS over TLS (2016) and HTTPS (2018) hid queries from eavesdroppers. Cloud services such as Route 53 (2010) turned DNS into a traffic-steering tool with health checks and latency routing, while public resolvers like Google Public DNS (2009) and Cloudflare’s 1.1.1.1 (2018) competed on speed and privacy.

choices.why: Handing each part of the tree to its owner removed the central bottleneck: a university or company can change its own names without asking anyone, and no single server holds everything.

choices.choice: Caching controlled by the data’s owner
choices.why: RFC 1034 says the source of the data should control the trade-off between lookup cost, update speed and accuracy. That is the TTL on every record, and why changes take time to reach everyone.

choices.choice: Typed records, not just host addresses
choices.why: Mockapetris designed for host addresses, mailbox data and “other as yet undetermined information”. That generality is why DNS now also carries mail routing, service discovery and domain verification.
A lookup and its answer usually fit in one UDP packet each (originally capped at 512 bytes), which keeps lookups fast and servers cheap. TCP is used for zone transfers and large answers.

timeline.text: Paul Mockapetris publishes the first DNS specs, RFC 882 and 883
Four UC Berkeley graduate students describe BIND, a DNS server for Unix
RFC 1034 and 1035 define DNS as it is still used
The root zone is signed with DNSSEC in July; Route 53 launches
DNS over HTTPS standardized (RFC 8484); Cloudflare launches 1.1.1.1
ICANN opens a new round of applications for top-level domains
